# Hormozi Lead Agencies — Learn the Skill, Then Leave

Agencies can add value — but not the way they want you to. You hire them to *learn new methods and new
platforms* (skills you keep forever and transfer to your team), then move on. This sub-skill runs that play.

**Method (authority):** `../_hormozi-shared/references/lead-getters.md` — the **## Agencies** section.
Read it before writing. Also read `../_hormozi-shared/references/decision-and-fidelity-rubric.md`.

## When to use
- "Should I hire an agency?", "which agency do I pick?", "how do I learn paid ads / a new platform fast?"
- As step 4 of the `hormozi-leads` chain (Lead Getters) — the one that teaches you skills you keep.

**Use a sibling instead when:** the lead getter is a customer (`hormozi-lead-referrals`), an employee you
train (`hormozi-lead-employees`), or an independent business promoting you (`hormozi-lead-affiliates`).

## Inputs
- The method/platform you want to learn (paid ads, outreach, content packaging/distribution).
- Whether you have money to spend right now (no money → agencies are out; learn by trial and error).
- Your team: who will absorb the skill and eventually beat the agency.

## Procedure
1. **Decide hire vs DIY** — good agencies cost money. No money → skip agencies, learn by trial and
   error. Money → use an agency for **exactly two things: learning new methods and learning new
   platforms** (they've already made the big mistakes; you skip to the "make money" part).
2. **Open with the learn-then-leave agreement** — start every relationship with a purpose *and* a
   deadline. Template: *"I want to do what you do in my business but don't know how. I'd like to work
   with you for 6 months to learn how. I'll pay extra for you to break down why you make the decisions
   you do. Then I'll train my team, and once they're good enough, move to a lower-cost consulting
   arrangement so you can still help. Are you opposed to this?"* Be willing to negotiate; if one refuses,
   move on. (Proven variant: a "good enough" agency to learn the platform, then an elite one to maximize it.)
3. **Pick the right agency — the 10-point checklist:** (1) someone you know got results with them;
   (2) prominent companies got results with them; (3) a waiting list (demand > supply); (4) a clear
   sales process with realistic expectations; (5) no short-term hacks — long-term strategy with
   timelines; (6) they tell you exactly what they need from you, when, and how; (7) *they* propose the
   meeting cadence and update methods; (8) they report in simple terms with clear cost-vs-results
   tracking; (9) they make a good offer judged on the four value elements (dream outcome · perceived
   likelihood · time delay · effort & sacrifice); (10) they are expensive (all good agencies are — but
   not all expensive ones are good). Talk to several more even if one agrees.
4. **Run learn-then-leave to the deadline** — you only get a fraction of their attention (worse as they
   add clients) while your team only improves. Compare your team's results to theirs; **once yours
   wins, cancel**, drop to discounted consulting until you're teaching them, then cut them loose and
   pour the money into scaling what you learned.

## Output contract
An **agency plan for this business**: the hire-vs-DIY call with its reason, the specific method/platform
to learn, the filled-in **agreement template** (with the deadline as `<placeholder>` if unset), a
**scored 10-point checklist** to vet candidates, and the exit trigger ("cancel once our team beats
theirs"). No fabricated agency prices or result claims — mark `<placeholder>` and cite the book's
figures by line ref.

## What we are intentionally NOT doing
- Not recommending a specific named agency or vendor — this produces the criteria and the play.
- Not the customer/employee/affiliate lead getters — those are the sibling sub-skills.
- Not signing contracts or negotiating on the user's behalf — flag terms for the user/counsel.

the learn-then-leave agreement template, and the 10-point pick-the-right-agency checklist. Encoded in
